programmes.d: The 1987 disappearance of Houston resident Tracy Jo Shine is recalled.
Armed with little else, police hoped that shoe impressions found at a Lansing, Michigan crime scene would put their investigation of Audrey Nichols' murder back on track.
Doctors cannot pinpoint the source of a businessman's illness.

A woman convicted of killing her mother in a car fire is granted a new trial. An expert witness has a different opinion as to how the fire started and, if proven, would clear the woman of any culpability.
After 6-year-old Michelle Lee Dorr went missing, her father confessed to murdering her.
In 1984, the body of college student Laura Salmon was found on a Middle Tennessee farm, covered with her own denim jeans as well as the jeans of the killer.
The 1996 investigation into 48-year-old Martha Hansen's murder is helped by a legal requirement.

A wealthy man and his wife were attacked by three masked men outside their luxurious Louisiana home. He was shot dead and she was forced to open their hidden safe. To solve the crime, police would have to find out who knew about the concealed safe.
The disappearance of a mail-order bride is suspicious when police learn of the husband's past wives.

On Christmas Eve 2005, a man's body is found burning near Baltimore. He's eventually identified as 26-year-old Wesley Person. Distinctive building materials from the 1930s play a crucial role in solving this case.
A jeweler's search through old sales records helps police find likely suspects in a couple's murder.

In 2002, a small community in upstate New York was devastated when Patty Wlasiuk died in a truck accident. But burdock seed pods found in her hair and on her clothes indicated that this was no accident — it was cold-blooded murder.
Garbage bag leads to a killer.
Responding to a 2008 garage fire, Illinois emergency response discovered a man crushed beneath a truck.
An investigation into the murder of Katie Poirier is stymied by the lack of a body.
In 1993, 82-year-old Kathryn Bishop was found dead in her Pennsylvania home. Tiny clues on the victim's body would tell police what happened that night.
The sensitive nose of a forensic examiner sniffs out murder.

A suspect's former lover comes forward with a fantastic tale of murder, mutilation and cremation. But there's no way to test the story's validity — until a plant pathologist and a dendrochronologist conduct tests where the cremation supposedly occurred.
An assailant avoids the law for 16 years due to a lack of evidence.

A young man was killed in a mysterious car crash, but the evidence at the scene led investigators to believe it was not an accident. Forensic science revealed what really happened and the truth devastated three families.
The only clue recovered from a shooting is a twelve-guage shotgun.

In 1996, police received a call from Darlie Routier telling them of her two sons' murders. The police found the killer by analyzing blood spatter, doing behavioral profiling and analyzing Darlie's 911 call.
A serial arsonist starts several fires that cause the deaths of three people.

When police in the Great Plains are called about a dead body, a background check on the victim leads them into a bizarre web of homeless drifters, cattle auctions and bad checks — all fronted by elderly couple Ray and Faye Copeland.
Computers aid the police and FBI in solving a string of crimes in St. Louis.
Witnesses saw a woman in the back of a truck, flailing her arms and screaming. When they found a jacket near a pool of blood, they knew what they had seen wasn't a joy ride.
Using an anonymous letter and geographical profiling, investigators close in on a serial rapist.
After a street fight takes the life of a national wrestling champion, police must determine if he was killed in cold blood or in self-defense.
A three-year-old develops a respiratory condition. His father has Alzheimers.
In 2001, Ginger Hayes and her infant son were abducted during a carjacking. The crime had been reported by a witness within minutes of occurrence.
A murder investigation in Florida crosses jurisdictions from New York and Jamaica.

A young woman suddenly becomes critically ill, eventually leaving her unable to walk. A bone marrow test reveals the cause: arsenic poisoning. Investigators must determine if the poisoning was caused by groundwater contamination or something sinister.
An examination of the 2002 DC area shooting spree that resulted in ten murders.
A woman convicted of killing her mother in a car fire is granted a new trial.

In 1971, John List left a note with the bodies of his mother, wife and three children in his mansion ballroom before disappearing completely. Detectives must solve the case, despite having only an outdated photograph of List.
Notepad points to kidnapper.

Police investigate a discarded sleeping bag containing bloody sneakers and a purse, which eventually leads to the body of a young woman. A mark found on the victim's body enables police to track the killer.
Debate over cause of death.

A mother of two young children was found dead in her bedroom. Her death was ruled a suicide — but when investigators learned she had almost died in a house fire three years earlier, they decided to take another look at the evidence.
A killer leaves the scene with the genetic fingerprint of his victim.

Three seemingly unrelated deaths prove to be serial murders. The killer had been careful; he used poison which had no taste or odor. Fortunately for investigators, it also had a unique chemical signature.
A vacuum-cleaner bag of microscopic paint-particles helps to identify a killer.
For 15 months, a serial killer was strangling prostitutes in Florida, then taunting police by leaving the bodies in plain sight. The only clues were a tire impression and some threads.
A mother of two vanishes after a shopping trip. Her body is discovered a month later.
A serial killer was on the loose and police had to find him before he struck again. Their most promising lead was an unusual one: a bloody fingerprint on the body of one of the victims.
A physics professor and NASA technology help to catch a killer.

Firefighters find an entire family dead inside their home in an apparent murder-suicide, but there are several inconsistent clues in the rubble. Could ballistics, a time card and some secret audiotapes unravel the mystery?
In 1993, worldwide attention focused on robberies which targeted tourists in Florida.
In 2003, St. Cloud teenager Jason MacLennan returned home after a night out with friends and discovered his father's body lying in a pool of blood.
At a murder scene, investigators find a shoe-print, several foreign hairs and unknown fingerprints.
A surgeon is stabbed to death and the most likely suspect is seen in a restaurant at the time of the murder.
A death in Pennsylvania is strikingly similar to one in North Carolina.
When a dedicated, well-respected teacher disappeared, police had to determine if she'd gone on vacation without telling anyone or if she was the victim of foul play.
A nurse learns that she has been deliberately infected with HIV.
When a little girl got sick and died, investigators were stumped. Was it an accident, an unexplained illness or murder?
A pregnant woman is found murdered in her air-conditioned bedroom.
A college senior was found raped and murdered near an unpaved footpath used by students to walk from one side of campus to the other.
Police were puzzled by an obscure print found at a murder crime scene.

The police investigate when a severed leg is discovered among garbage. Conventional means of identifying the victim are impossible, leading investigators to rely on DNA, forensic anthropology and toxicology.
A man is found dead in his home and his ex-wife has an almost perfect alibi.
It was a tragic twist of fate. Just days after a woman sold her home and moved to a modest trailer, a fire took both the trailer and her life. But the autopsy proved this was no accident.
A union official is executed in his home not long after a strike by the union membership.
When Chris Ochoa confessed to the 1988 rape and murder of Nancy DePriest, the case was closed. 8 years later, Achim Marino confessed to the same crime. Can DNA evidence identify the real perpetrator?
In 1988, the body of a young woman was discovered in an Ohio river.
Crystal Faye Todd's case is examined; the popular high school student was raped and murdered.

When a policeman's house goes up in flames, experts suspect arson. The officer whose home was torched arrests low-level drug dealer James Wren, who confesses. But when the suspect vanishes, investigators question the authenticity of the confession.
Police discovered the body of Douglas Beamish's estranged wife.

When the wife of a well-known dentist is found dead, police struggle to identify a suspect. Some fibers and a study of the weather patterns on the night of the murder break the case open and reveal the killer.
More than 700 Oregonians contracted food poisoning from a unique strain of salmonella in 1984.

The body of a young woman was found a mile from her abandoned car. Police were especially concerned when they realized the victim had come to them for protection just two weeks earlier after a road rage incident.
A woman is found dead from a gunshot wound and police suspect her husband.
In this classic episode of Forensic Files, the longest-running true crime series in television history, a serial bomber targets a judge, two attorneys and even a courthouse.
In 1995, the founder of American Atheists disappeared with $500,000 in gold coins.
In 2008, the body of Colorado real estate developer Alan Helmick was found by his wife, Miriam, who then became the prime suspect.
Two eyewitnesses may hold the key to the death of a motorcycle gang member.

While vacationing in California, Earl Morris learns that his wife has gone missing from their Arizona home. The search for Ruby Morris involves dozens of investigators and scientists — and even the Coast Guard.
In 1984, a passerby finds the torso of a woman in a cardboard box.

In 1996, Derrick Duehren returned to find his Oregon home burned to the ground. His wife's charred remains were later found in the rubble. Investigators set out to determine if it was an unfortunate accident or murder.
A victim's knowledge of forensic evidence leads police to her abductor.

A woman disappears and her husband becomes the prime suspect — especially after police find a huge bloodstain on the carpet of their bedroom. When they spray the bedroom with Luminol, they discover it was awash with blood spatter.
The police investigate when a severed leg is discovered among garbage.
When two boys are brutally attacked, investigators rely on evidence fished out of a nearby pond. It became the first case where diatom analysis was used to place a suspect at the scene of the crime.
In a 1992 murder case, the autopsy of a cremated body turns up telltale clues of foul play.
In 1999, 9-year-old Valiree Jackson vanished on her way to school near Spokane. Her father, Brad Jackson, reported the disappearance and the entire community started searching for her abductor.
Forensic developments reveal new facts in the case of a man convicted of sexual assault.

When an elderly couple died in a suspicious house fire, their son became the prime suspect. Investigators turned to forensic science to determine if the fire had been set deliberately, or if it was an unfortunate accident.
The murder of a couple puzzles investigators until the victims' dog leads police to the killer.

In 1988, the body of a young woman was discovered in an Ohio river. Most of the evidence had been washed away, but the victim's 6-year-old son unwittingly told investigators all they needed to know — without saying a word. The clue was in his genes.
Soon after becoming pregnant, firefighter Michelle Baker's health quickly deteriorates.
When a hit-and-run accident claimed the life of a high school athlete, everyone in town mourned his passing. Finding the killer was a long shot at best.
In the 1980s, a trio of unsolved murders occurred in Wichita Falls, Texas.
The body of 16-year-old Leanne Tiernan was discovered nine months after she disappeared. Forensic scientists found clues that painted a virtual portrait of her killer.
An abandoned, still-running car leads investigators to a body with unusual marks.
In 2008, college co-ed Jenna Verhaalen was found dead in her Bryan, Texas apartment. Petechial hemorrhages in her eyes indicated that she was strangled.
Police uncover deleted computer files during an investigation.
By using techniques she saw on forensic science TV shows, a mother determines who was responsible for the accident that permanently injured her 4-year-old daughter.
A suspicious neighbor gives police a break in a cold case.
